title: WHO WAS OG, KING OF BASHAN?
paragraphs:
WHO WAS OG, KING OF BASHAN?
The Giant Everyone Feared… and the Forgotten Story That Proves No Scandal, No Giant, and No Past Is Bigger Than Jesus
Some names in Scripture make people stop.
Moses.
David.
Paul.
But then there is a name hidden deep inside the pages of the Old Testament that feels almost mysterious.
Og.
A giant king.
A ruler of Bashan.
A man whose reputation was so terrifying that God Himself had to tell Israel not to be afraid before the battle even began.
Yet most believers know almost nothing about him.
Who was Og, King of Bashan?
Why does Scripture mention his enormous bed?
Why did Moses record his defeat so carefully?
And why does his story still matter for every person carrying shame, fear, addiction, failure, regret, or a past they believe can never be overcome?
Because the story of Og is not ultimately about a giant.
It is about a greater King.
It is about the God who specializes in taking impossible situations and rewriting them through His grace.
It is about Jesus.
And it is about you.
The first time we encounter Og, he appears as one of the final obstacles standing between God's people and their inheritance.
The Bible tells us:
“Then we turned and went up the way to Bashan: and Og the king of Bashan came out against us, he and all his people, to battle at Edrei.” (Deuteronomy 3:1)
Imagine the scene.
Israel had already experienced miraculous victories.
Yet this enemy was different.
His reputation preceded him.
His kingdom was powerful.
His people were warriors.
And Og himself belonged to a remnant of giants.
Scripture specifically states:
“For only Og king of Bashan remained of the remnant of the Rephaim.” (Deuteronomy 3:11)
The Hebrew word is רְפָאִים (Rephaim).
Throughout the Old Testament, the Rephaim are described as a race of unusually large and powerful people.
Whether every detail of their stature can be measured precisely is debated among scholars, but Scripture leaves no doubt about the central point:
These were individuals whose size and strength inspired fear.
Og represented the last major remnant of that terrifying legacy east of the Jordan.
Then God spoke.
And everything changed.
“Do not fear him.”
In Hebrew:
אַל־תִּירָא אֹתוֹ
(Al-Tira Oto)
Do not fear him.
Not because Og was small.
Not because the threat was imaginary.
Not because Israel was strong.
But because God had already determined the outcome.
“And the LORD said unto me, Fear him not: for I will deliver him, and all his people, and his land, into thy hand.” (Numbers 21:34)
This is one of the most repeated commands in all Scripture.
Do not fear.
Not because giants do not exist.
But because God remains greater than every giant.
That truth reaches far beyond Bashan.
Many people reading this are fighting giants right now.
Not physical giants.
Emotional giants.
Spiritual giants.
Hidden giants.
The giant of addiction.
The giant of pornography.
The giant of depression.
The giant of shame.
The giant of betrayal.
The giant of anxiety.
The giant of failure.
The giant of a scandal that still haunts your name.
Some have spent years believing those giants are too large to defeat.
Og's story says otherwise.
The battle itself was surprisingly short in the biblical record.
God delivered Og into Israel's hands.
The giant fell.
His kingdom fell.
His power ended.
The obstacle that looked impossible became another testimony of God's faithfulness.
Then Moses includes a detail that has fascinated readers for centuries.
“Behold, his bedstead was a bedstead of iron; is it not in Rabbah of the children of Ammon? Nine cubits was the length thereof, and four cubits the breadth of it.” (Deuteronomy 3:11)
The measurements translate to approximately thirteen and a half feet long and six feet wide.
Some scholars argue the measurement reflects the bed itself rather than Og's exact height.
Others suggest it was a royal display object emphasizing his enormous stature.
Either way, Moses was making a point.
Og was not a myth.
He was real.
His power was real.
His influence was real.
His threat was real.
And God defeated him anyway.
That detail matters.
Because faith is not pretending problems are small.
Faith is believing God remains bigger.
Many people misunderstand biblical courage.
Biblical courage is not denying reality.
Biblical courage is acknowledging reality while trusting God more.
That is exactly what happened at Bashan.
But there is something even deeper hidden beneath the story.
Throughout Scripture, giant enemies often symbolize humanity's impossible condition.
Sin itself is a giant.
Death is a giant.
Judgment is a giant.
No human being can defeat those enemies through personal effort.
The Apostle Paul writes:
The Greek word for sin is ἁμαρτία (hamartia).
It literally carries the idea of missing the mark.
Every person has missed it.
Every person has failed.
Every person carries a story that contains brokenness.
That is where the Gospel enters.
Because Jesus confronted the giant nobody else could defeat.
At the cross, Christ faced sin.
At the cross, Christ faced death.
At the cross, Christ faced the judgment we deserved.
Then three days later, He walked out of the tomb.
The greatest giant in history fell before the greatest King in history.
This is why the Gospel is not self-improvement.
It is rescue.
Not moral polishing.
Redemption.
Not behavior management.
Resurrection.
Jesus does not merely help people fight giants.
He conquers them.
And perhaps that is why Og's story continues to resonate thousands of years later.
Every human heart knows what it feels like to stand before something larger than itself.
A mistake too big.
A wound too deep.
A failure too public.
A scandal too devastating.
Yet the entire Bible points toward one breathtaking reality:
Grace is greater.
The New Testament word for grace is χάρις (charis).
Undeserved favor.
Undeserved kindness.
Undeserved mercy.
The kind of mercy that rewrites stories.
The kind of mercy that takes persecutors like Paul and turns them into apostles.
The kind of mercy that takes adulterers, thieves, doubters, addicts, outcasts, failures, and broken people and transforms them into testimonies.
The kind of mercy that takes your story and rewrites it too.
That is the heartbeat of everything we do at Gospel Warrior.
Because every day people arrive carrying giants.
Some arrive carrying shame.
Some arrive carrying secret sin.
Some arrive carrying wounds they have hidden for years.
Some arrive convinced God could never use them.
And every day we point them to the same answer:
Jesus Christ.
Not religion.
Not performance.
Not perfection.
Jesus.
The Savior who still rewrites stories.
The Savior who still rescues.
The Savior who still transforms.
The Savior who still turns scandals into testimonies.
What giant are you trusting Jesus to help you overcome?
"Christ is still healing me"
if God is still writing your story.
if you refuse to give up on your faith.
Your testimony may encourage someone else who feels alone.
Sometimes one share becomes the answer to someone's prayer.
Because the giant was never the end of the story.
God was.
And He still is.
The same God who defeated Og.
The same God who raised Jesus from the dead.
The same God who can redeem your past, restore your future, and rewrite your story through His grace.
The giant looked invincible until God stepped onto the battlefield.
The cross looked like defeat until the stone rolled away.
